query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace level of boron (≈0.1–0.5 at%) into an already lightweight, Al-modified TaNbVTi-based refractory high-entropy alloy will form nanoscale boron‐rich precipitates or promote beneficial grain boundary segregation that impedes high-temperature dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding. This microstructural modification should increase the high-temperature yield strength while retaining the intrinsically low density and satisfactory room-temperature ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A lightweight, single-phase BCC TaNbVTi-based refractory high-entropy alloy modified with Al (which lowers the density to around 7.75 g/cm³) that currently exhibits a good balance of room-temperature strength and ductility.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a trace amount of boron (approximately 0.1–0.5 atomic percent) during alloy fabrication (e.g., via mechanical alloying and subsequent consolidation by spark plasma sintering).
generation.conditions: Mechanical performance evaluated at room temperature as well as under high-temperature conditions (900–1200 °C) under uniaxial compression/tensile loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of finely dispersed boron-rich precipitates and/or enhanced boron segregation along grain boundaries within the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The added boron is expected to segregate preferentially to grain boundaries and/or form coherent nano-precipitates, which act as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding at elevated temperatures. This additional barrier mechanism enhances high-temperature yield strength, yet the limited boron content and its controlled distribution prevent negative impacts on room-temperature ductility or density.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the boron-doped alloy is predicted to exhibit an improvement of on the order of 10–20% in high-temperature yield strength without a significant change in room-temperature mechanical properties or density.
generation.baseline: The performance metrics (yield strength, ductility, density) of the un-doped, Al-modified TaNbVTi-based alloy as reported in previous studies.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only within a narrow boron doping range; excessive boron could lead to the formation of coarse brittle phases or excessive grain boundary embrittlement, which would compromise room-temperature performance.
generation.uncertainty: While prior work (PMC9586648) showed that trace B or C additions can strengthen MoNbTaW alloys via grain boundary improvements and other studies (PMC7516739) have achieved lightweight benefits via Al addition, the exact boron solubility, precipitate nature, and its quantitative effect on the TaNbVTi-based system remain uncertain and require experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the Al-modified TaNbVTi alloy using identical processing conditions—one set with a trace boron addition (≈0.3 at% as a representative mid-value) and one set without. Perform microstructural characterization (using TEM and EDS) to establish the presence and distribution of boron-induced precipitates or grain boundary segregation. Then, conduct standardized uniaxial tensile and compressive tests at room temperature and in the high-temperature range (900–1200 °C) to measure yield strengths and ductility.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (TEM/EDS) for identifying boron-rich phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped alloy fails to show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than a 10% increase) in high-temperature yield strength compared to the baseline un-doped alloy, or if its room-temperature mechanical performance or density is adversely affected, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Xu et al. [] reduced the density of the Ti50-xAlxV20Nb20Mo10 RHEA from 6.102 g/cm3 (Ti40Al10V20Nb20Mo10) to 5.876 g/cm3 (Ti30Al20V20Nb20Mo10) by adjusting the Al content, and the room-temperature specific yield strength increased from 147.49 MPa*cm3/g to 202.01 MPa*cm3/g. Although the density and specific strength of these alloys are significantly improved after the addition of aluminum, their plasticity is generally reduced. Therefore, choosing a refractory high-entropy alloy with both high strength and high plasticity as a matrix, and then reducing its density by adding light elements such as Al, is an effective method to obtain structural materials with high strength, low density, and good plasticity. The recently reported TaNbVTi alloy meets the requirements of the matrix very well []. Furthermore, Yang et al. [] reported that the arc-melted NbTiVTaAl0.25 HEA has a low density of 8.78 g/cm3 and reasonable plasticity greater than 50%. Nevertheless, the yield strength of this alloy is only 1330 MPa (specific strength of 151.48 MPa*cm3/g), which has the possibility of further improvement compared with most refractory high-entropy alloys.

After the first development of RHEAs in 2010, over 150 kinds of compositions have been reported, with their potential for use in high-temperature applications such as gas turbine engines and rocket nozzles. Various studies focused on ductility enhancement [,], better oxidation resistance [], and nuclear reactor material applications [,]. According to a review by Senkov et al. [], the only alloys to pass high-temperature compression tests at 1600°C were MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW. The main reason for the difficulty to perform compression tests at extremely high temperatures is the lack of suitable material as a jig material that provides high strength at extremely high temperatures. Recently, Wang et al. strengthened the grain boundary of an MoNbTaW-refractory high-entropy alloy through doping with B or C in trace amount, which simultaneously increases room-temperature strength and toughness []. This study provides a good strategy to increase the ductility of RHEAs by doping suitable elements.
